claim: V1 and V2b interneurons (INs) are essential for the production of an alternating flexor–extensor motor output.
source: V1 and V2b interneurons (INs) are essential for the production of an alternating flexor–extensor motor output.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational claim of the study.

claim: Ablation of V1 INs results in limb hyperflexion.
source: Ablation of V1 INs results in limb hyperflexion, suggesting that V1 IN-derived inhibition is needed for proper extension movements of the limb.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 3, 4, and 6.

claim: V1 IN-derived inhibition is needed for proper extension movements of the limb.
source: Ablation of V1 INs results in limb hyperflexion, suggesting that V1 IN-derived inhibition is needed for proper extension movements of the limb.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hyperflexion phenotype observed upon V1 IN ablation.

claim: The loss of V2b INs results in hindlimb hyperextension.
source: The loss of V2b INs results in hindlimb hyperextension and a delay in the transition from stance phase to swing phase, demonstrating V2b INs are required for the timely initiation and execution of limb flexion movements.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 3, 4, and 6.

claim: The loss of V2b INs results in a delay in the transition from stance phase to swing phase.
source: The loss of V2b INs results in hindlimb hyperextension and a delay in the transition from stance phase to swing phase, demonstrating V2b INs are required for the timely initiation and execution of limb flexion movements.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by EMG and kinematic data in Figure 6.

claim: V2b INs are required for the timely initiation and execution of limb flexion movements.
source: The loss of V2b INs results in hindlimb hyperextension and a delay in the transition from stance phase to swing phase, demonstrating V2b INs are required for the timely initiation and execution of limb flexion movements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hyperextension and delayed stance-to-swing transition observed upon V2b IN ablation.

claim: There is a bias in the innervation of flexor- and extensor-related motor neurons by V1 and V2b INs.
source: Our findings also reveal a bias in the innervation of flexor- and extensor-related motor neurons by V1 and V2b INs that likely contributes to their differential actions on flexion–extension movements.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by anatomical data in Figure 8.

claim: The bias in innervation of motor neurons by V1 and V2b INs likely contributes to their differential actions on flexion–extension movements.
source: Our findings also reveal a bias in the innervation of flexor- and extensor-related motor neurons by V1 and V2b INs that likely contributes to their differential actions on flexion–extension movements.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking anatomical findings to functional outcomes.

claim: All motor behaviors rely on the reciprocal actions of flexor and extensor muscles around each limb joint.
source: Charles Sherrington (1906) first demonstrated that all such motor behaviors rely on the reciprocal actions of flexor and extensor muscles around each limb joint and that terrestrial animals require reciprocal inhibition to move and articulate their limbs.
evidence: This is attributed to Sherrington's work and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Terrestrial animals require reciprocal inhibition to move and articulate their limbs.
source: Charles Sherrington (1906) first demonstrated that all such motor behaviors rely on the reciprocal actions of flexor and extensor muscles around each limb joint and that terrestrial animals require reciprocal inhibition to move and articulate their limbs.
evidence: This is attributed to Sherrington's work and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Reciprocal flexor–extensor motor activity is produced by inhibitory neurons in the spinal cord.
source: It is known that reciprocal flexor–extensor motor activity is produced by inhibitory neurons in the spinal cord, many of which appear to be core components of the locomotor central pattern generator (CPG) (reviewed in Kiehn, 2006; Goulding, 2009; Grillner and Jessell, 2009; Arber, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by multiple review citations.

claim: Many inhibitory neurons in the spinal cord appear to be core components of the locomotor central pattern generator (CPG).
source: It is known that reciprocal flexor–extensor motor activity is produced by inhibitory neurons in the spinal cord, many of which appear to be core components of the locomotor central pattern generator (CPG) (reviewed in Kiehn, 2006; Goulding, 2009; Grillner and Jessell, 2009; Arber, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by multiple review citations.

claim: Reciprocal Ia inhibitory interneurons (IaINs) are activated by muscle spindle afferents and inhibit antagonist motor neurons.
source: The most prominent of these are reciprocal Ia inhibitory interneurons (IaINs), which are activated by muscle spindle afferents and inhibit antagonist motor neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about IaINs.

claim: IaINs are rhythmically active during locomotion.
source: IaINs are rhythmically active during locomotion (Feldman and Orlovsky, 1975; Pratt and Jordan, 1987) and scratching (Deliagina and Orlovsky, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IaINs are rhythmically active during scratching.
source: IaINs are rhythmically active during locomotion (Feldman and Orlovsky, 1975; Pratt and Jordan, 1987) and scratching (Deliagina and Orlovsky, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Peak IaIN activity coincides with the phase in which antagonist motor neurons are hyperpolarized.
source: Peak IaIN activity coincides with the phase in which antagonist motor neurons are hyperpolarized (Pratt and Jordon, 1987; Geertsen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The V1 and V2b IN populations are both heterogeneous, being made up of multiple physiological cell types including Renshaw cells (V1 INs), IaINs (V1 and V2b INs) and putative IbINs (V2b INs).
source: The V1 and V2b IN populations are both heterogeneous, being made up of multiple physiological cell types including Renshaw cells (V1 INs), IaINs (V1 and V2b INs) and putative IbINs (V2b INs) (Sapir et al., 2004; Alvarez et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2014), as well as other as yet unidentified inhibitory cell types.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The composite activities of the V1 and V2b INs are required to secure flexor–extensor alternation in the in vitro neonatal spinal cord and in newborn mice.
source: Recently, we have found that the composite activities of the V1 and V2b INs are required to secure flexor–extensor alternation in the in vitro neonatal spinal cord and in newborn mice (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Cells with the features of IaINs are derived from both V1 and V2b INs.
source: This finding is consistent with our demonstration that cells with the features of IaINs are derived from both V1 and V2b INs and that disynaptic reciprocal inhibition is only abolished when both of these populations are functionally inactivated (Wang et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Disynaptic reciprocal inhibition is only abolished when both V1 and V2b populations are functionally inactivated.
source: This finding is consistent with our demonstration that cells with the features of IaINs are derived from both V1 and V2b INs and that disynaptic reciprocal inhibition is only abolished when both of these populations are functionally inactivated (Wang et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: En1 and Gata3 selectively mark spinal V1 and V2b INs, respectively.
source: Although En1 and Gata3 selectively mark spinal V1 and V2b INs, respectively, both genes are expressed elsewhere in the midbrain, medulla and cerebellum, and in non-neuronal tissues (Davis and Joyner, 1988; van Doorninck et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: En1 and Gata3 are expressed in the midbrain, medulla and cerebellum, and in non-neuronal tissues.
source: Although En1 and Gata3 selectively mark spinal V1 and V2b INs, respectively, both genes are expressed elsewhere in the midbrain, medulla and cerebellum, and in non-neuronal tissues (Davis and Joyner, 1988; van Doorninck et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: Genetic protocols that employ En1 and Gata3 regulatory sequences alone to silence or ablate V1 and V2b INs cause perinatal death.
source: Consequently, genetic protocols that employ En1 and Gata3 regulatory sequences alone to silence or ablate V1 and V2b INs cause perinatal death (Gosgnach et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Cdx2-FlpO transgene displayed little or no recombination in anterior neural structures including the cortex, basal forebrain, midbrain, pons/medulla, and cerebellum.
source: Most importantly, the Cdx2-FlpO transgene displayed little or no recombination in anterior neural structures including the cortex, basal forebrain, midbrain, pons/medulla, and cerebellum.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section describing the characterization of the Cdx2-FlpO transgene.

claim: In P15 En1Cre; Cdx2-FlpO; R26ds-nlslacZ mice, nlslacZ expression in V1 INs spanned mid-cervical to sacral levels of the spinal cord.
source: In P15 En1Cre; Cdx2-FlpO; R26ds-nlslacZ mice, we observed a caudal pattern of nlslacZ expression in V1 INs that spanned mid-cervical to sacral levels of the spinal cord (Figure 1C; data not shown).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: GFP reporter expression was activated in virtually all V1-derived cells at lumbosacral levels when using the R26ds-HTB reporter.
source: When a R26ds-HTB reporter mouse (Stam et al., 2012) was used to assess the extent of En1Cre and Cdx2-FlpO recombination in V1 INs, GFP reporter expression was activated in virtually all V1-derived cells at lumbosacral levels (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1E,F.

claim: Fewer than 20% of the V1 INs at upper- to mid-cervical levels displayed Flp-mediated recombination.
source: By contrast, fewer than 20% of the V1 INs at upper- to mid-cervical levels displayed Flp-mediated recombination (Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1D,F.

claim: GFP was not detected in other supraspinal populations of En1-derived neurons.
source: Most importantly, GFP was not detected in other supraspinal populations of En1-derived neurons, demonstrating the Cdx2-FlpO transgene selectively and efficiently targets V1 INs in the caudal spinal cord when used in combination with En1Cre.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section.

claim: V1 INs were depleted by >90% in the thoracic, lumbar, and sacral spinal cord of En1Cre; Cdx2-FlpO; Maptds-DTR; Ai6 mice following DTX treatment.
source: Whereas V1 INs were largely spared at upper cervical levels (Figure 2A,B), they were depleted by >90% in the thoracic, lumbar, and sacral spinal cord of En1Cre; Cdx2-FlpO; Maptds-DTR; Ai6 mice (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2C,D.

claim: Calbindin+ Renshaw cells were largely missing from the caudal spinal cord following V1 IN ablation.
source: Calbindin+ Renshaw cells, which are derived from En1+ progenitors (Sapir et al., 2004), were also largely missing from the caudal spinal cord (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2E,F.

claim: Dorsal calbindin+ neurons that are not derived from En1+ progenitors were still present in normal numbers following V1 IN ablation.
source: By contrast, dorsal calbindin+ neurons that are not derived from En1+ progenitors were still present in normal numbers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Motor neurons and cholinergic V0c INs were unaffected by the DTR-dependent ablation of V1 INs.
source: To confirm the specificity of V1 IN cell killing, sections from control and V1 IN-ablated cords were stained with an antibody to choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) to visualize motor neurons and cholinergic V0c INs. Both populations were unaffected by the DTR-dependent ablation of V1 INs (Figure 2A–D, data not shown).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2A–D.

claim: There was no reduction in the number of Chx10+ V2a INs following V1 IN ablation.
source: Moreover, there was no reduction in the number of Chx10+ V2a INs, a prominent population of excitatory neurons that are intermingled with V1 INs in lamina VII (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2G,H.

claim: There was no change in the integrity of the spinal cord following V1 IN ablation.
source: Further histological analysis revealed no change in the integrity of the spinal cord following V1 IN ablation (Figure 2I,J) nor was there any reduction in neuronal cell numbers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2I,J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: DTR-mediated cell killing is highly selective and cell autonomous.
source: These results agree with other studies showing DTR-mediated cell killing is highly selective and cell autonomous (Buch et al., 2005; Hatori et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The hindlimbs of P7 DTX-treated En1Cre; Cdx2-FlpO; Maptds-DTR V1 IN-ablated pups remained flexed when suspended by their tails.
source: Whereas control P7 pups flexed and extended their hindlimbs when suspended by their tails (Figure 3A), the hindlimbs of P7 DTX-treated En1Cre; Cdx2-FlpO; Maptds-DTR V1 IN-ablated pups remained flexed (Figure 3B), even though their forelimbs were able to extend and display a full range of stepping movements (Figure 3B, asterisk).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: P7 Gata3Cre; Cdx2-FlpO; Maptds-DTR V2b IN-ablated mice maintained their hindlimbs in an extended state when suspended by their tail.
source: In contrast to control mice and V1 IN-ablated mice, P7 Gata3Cre; Cdx2-FlpO; Maptds-DTR V2b IN-ablated mice maintained their hindlimbs in an extended state when suspended by their tail (Figure 3C), even though they were still able to flex and extend their forelimbs.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: V1 IN-ablated animals displayed very little hindlimb movement during L-DOPA-induced airstepping.
source: Kinematic analysis revealed strong rhythmic stepping in both the forelimbs and hindlimbs of control animals (Figure 4). By contrast, V1 IN-ablated animals displayed very little hindlimb movement, in contrast to the forelimbs that showed a normal range of motion.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 4.

claim: The maximal opening of the ankle joint in V1 IN-ablated animals was less than 80° compared to 145° for control animals.
source: Moreover, the maximal opening of the ankle joint in these animals was less than 80° compared to 145° for control animals (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 4B,C.

claim: The hindlimbs of V2b IN-ablated mice remained extended during L-DOPA-induced airstepping and displayed very little in the way of flexion movements.
source: When V2b IN-ablated mice were induced to airwalk and analyzed in a similar manner, they displayed robust rhythmic forelimb stepping movements (Figure 4, right panels). By contrast, the hindlimbs of these mice remained extended and displayed very little in the way of flexion movements.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 4.

claim: The angle of the ankle joint in V2b IN-ablated mice was not reduced below 130° during airstepping.
source: However, as the angle of the ankle joint was not reduced below 130° (Figure 4C), it appears that the hindlimb locomotor CPG is unable to elicit strong flexion movements in the absence of V2b inhibition.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 4C.

claim: Control P7 mice displayed a regular alternating pattern of EMG activity in TA and GS muscles during L-DOPA-induced air-stepping.
source: Control mice displayed a regular alternating pattern of EMG activity in both muscles (Figure 5A) in which there was little or no overlap in TA and GS burst activity.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 5A.

claim: The GS extensor phase increased proportionately with longer step periods in control mice, while the TA flexor burst period was constant across all stepping speeds.
source: The GS extensor phase was also seen to increase proportionately with longer step periods, while the TA flexor burst period was constant across all stepping speeds (Figure 5A,D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 5A,D.

claim: Changes in duration of the extensor/stance phase are preferentially responsible for lengthening or shortening the step cycle.
source: This is in strong agreement with previous studies performed in rodents and cats (Grillner, 1975; Halbertsma, 1983; Juvin et al., 2007; Frigon and Gossard, 2009) showing that changes in duration of the extensor/stance phase are preferentially responsible for lengthening or shortening the step cycle.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: V1 IN-ablated mice consistently displayed a marked increase in the duration of the TA burst.
source: V1 IN-ablated mice consistently displayed a marked increase in the duration of the TA burst, with the TA muscle remaining active for a proportionately longer period of each step cycle as compared to the GS muscle (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: Depleting V1 IN inhibition causes a preferential degradation of inhibition to TA flexor motor neurons.
source: This finding is consistent with the idea that depleting V1 IN inhibition causes a preferential degradation of inhibition to TA flexor motor neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the increased TA burst duration observed in V1 IN-ablated mice.

claim: The duration of GS extensor muscle activity was markedly elongated in V2b IN-depleted mice during airstepping.
source: V2b IN-depleted mice displayed a strikingly different pattern of EMG activity during airstepping. In addition to an aggregate slowing of the motor rhythm, the duration of GS extensor muscle activity was markedly elongated (Figure 5C–E) when compared to control and V1 IN-ablated animals.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 5C–E.

claim: The slowing of the motor rhythm following the loss of V2b INs can largely be attributed to the increased duration of GS extensor activity.
source: This slowing of the motor rhythm following the loss of V2b INs can largely be attributed to the increased duration of GS extensor activity, as the TA flexor bursts were similar in length to those seen in control mice (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 5C,D.

claim: A flexor-dominant motor rhythm emerges when V1 INs are deleted.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that a flexor-dominant motor rhythm emerges when V1 INs are deleted, while the loss of V2b INs gives rise to an extensor-dominant motor rhythm.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the EMG data from V1 IN-ablated mice.

claim: The loss of V2b INs gives rise to an extensor-dominant motor rhythm.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that a flexor-dominant motor rhythm emerges when V1 INs are deleted, while the loss of V2b INs gives rise to an extensor-dominant motor rhythm.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the EMG data from V2b IN-ablated mice.

claim: There was a significant increase in the number and frequency of skipped or deleted GS and TA bursts in air-stepping juvenile mice lacking V1 or V2b INs.
source: Further analysis of the EMG profiles of V1- and V2b-IN-ablated mice revealed a significant increase in the number and frequency of skipped or deleted GS and TA bursts in air-stepping juvenile mice (Figure 5A, arrowheads).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 5A.

claim: TA deletions were prevalent in V2b IN-ablated pups.
source: Whereas TA deletions were prevalent in V2b IN-ablated pups (Figure 5A, right panel, arrowheads), mice lacking V1 INs displayed a strong bias toward deletions in GS EMG activity (Figure 5, middle panel, arrowhead).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Mice lacking V1 INs displayed a strong bias toward deletions in GS EMG activity.
source: Whereas TA deletions were prevalent in V2b IN-ablated pups (Figure 5A, right panel, arrowheads), mice lacking V1 INs displayed a strong bias toward deletions in GS EMG activity (Figure 5, middle panel, arrowhead).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 5.

claim: Inhibition from V1 and V2b INs facilitates the transition from swing to stance and from stance to swing, respectively.
source: The increased frequency of deletions in the V1- and V2b-IN-ablated mice (Figure 5D) coupled with the changes in phase duration (Figure 5C), strongly suggest that inhibition from V1 and V2b INs facilitates the transition from swing to stance and from stance to swing, respectively.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the deletion patterns and phase duration changes.

claim: The deletions in both V1- and V2b-IN-ablated mice fall into the non-resetting category.
source: Our observation that the deletions in both V1- and V2b-IN-ablated mice fall into the non-resetting category strongly suggests that both of these genetically defined cell populations are involved in pattern formation rather than rhythm generation (Lafreniere-Roula and McCrea, 2005).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: V1 and V2b INs are involved in pattern formation rather than rhythm generation.
source: Our observation that the deletions in both V1- and V2b-IN-ablated mice fall into the non-resetting category strongly suggests that both of these genetically defined cell populations are involved in pattern formation rather than rhythm generation (Lafreniere-Roula and McCrea, 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the non-resetting deletion pattern.

claim: V1 IN-ablated mice displayed marked deficits in their gait, including a persistent hyperflexion of the hindlimbs during walking.
source: V1 IN-ablated mice still displayed marked deficits in their gait, including a persistent hyperflexion of the hindlimbs during walking, which was particularly prominent in the mid-swing and early stance phases of the step cycle (Figure 6A,B, middle panel).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 6A,B.

claim: V1 IN-ablated mice flexed their hindlimbs faster during the swing phase.
source: Furthermore, V1 IN-ablated mice flexed their hindlimbs faster during the swing phase indicating that they are no longer able to properly modulate the speed and/or force of their flexion movements (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 6C.

claim: The EMG analysis of V1 IN-ablated mice revealed marked changes in the duration and co-activity of TA and GS muscle activity.
source: The EMG analysis of V1 IN-ablated mice revealed marked changes in the duration and co-activity of TA and GS muscle activity. These included (1) a persistent broadening of TA muscle activity, (2) an overlap in GS and TA burst activity during the transition from stance to swing, and (3) an increase in GS activity at the end of the stance phase (Figure 6D, middle panel, asterisk; Figure 6—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 6D and supplementary figures.

claim: The co-activation of the TA and GS muscles was even more pronounced during swimming in V1 IN-ablated mice.
source: The co-activation of the TA and GS muscles was even more pronounced during swimming with EMG analysis revealing synchronous TA and GS muscle activity (Figure 6E, middle panel, asterisk) that causes the extension of the hindlimbs to be aborted during the power stroke.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 6E.

claim: V1 IN-ablated mice displayed a prominent rear paw overshoot during walking.
source: In addition to the hyperflexion phenotype, V1 IN-ablated mice displayed a prominent rear paw overshoot during walking (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The locomotor phenotype that persists in mice lacking V2b INs was much milder than in V1 IN-ablated mice.
source: In contrast to V1 IN-ablated mice, the locomotor phenotype that persists in mice lacking V2b INs was much milder, with the most notable change being a prolongation of the stance phase that results in overextension of the ankle joint during walking (Figure 6A, right panel, arrowhead).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 6A.

claim: A second ectopic burst of GS motor activity occurs as the limb is transitioning from stance to swing in V2b IN-ablated mice.
source: EMG analysis revealed the likely cause of this delay, namely a second ectopic burst of GS motor activity as the limb is transitioning from stance to swing (Figure 6D, right panel, asterisk).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 6D.

claim: The delay in initiating flexion was not observed when V2b IN-ablated mice were swimming.
source: The delay in initiating flexion was not observed when the mice were swimming nor did we detect any marked differences in TA and GS EMG activity between control and V2b IN-ablated mice during swimming (Figure 6E, right panel).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 6E.

claim: The depletion of V1 INs resulted in ectopic IP and TA muscle EMG activity within 5 days of DTX treatment in adult mice.
source: Whereas control mice (n = 5 animals) displayed a highly reproducible pattern of EMG activity both before and after DTX treatment, with the iliopsoas (IP) and TA muscles only being active during the swing phase of the step cycle (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, upper left panel), the depletion of V1 INs (n = 6 animals) resulted in ectopic IP and TA muscle EMG activity within 5 days of DTX treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, upper panel).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Ectopic TA and IP muscle activity was even more pronounced 7 days after DTX treatment in V1 IN-ablated adult mice.
source: This ectopic TA and IP muscle activity was even more pronounced 7 days after DTX treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C, upper panel), with the TA muscle being co-active during stance with the GS muscle (see bars).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The co-activation of the TA and IP muscles during stance restricts the hip and ankle joints from opening during walking in V1 IN-ablated mice.
source: We posit that the co-activation of the TA and IP muscles during stance constitutes the underlying mechanism that restricts the hip and ankle joints from opening during walking, and it also contributes to the postural changes that occur in V1 IN-ablated mice following DTX treatment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EMG and kinematic data.

claim: There was no increase in GS activity during the swing/flexor phase in V1 IN-ablated mice.
source: By contrast, there was no increase in GS activity during the swing/flexor phase indicating the loss of V1 INs has an effect on ankle flexor but not extensor activity during walking.
evidence: This is stated directly based on EMG analysis.

claim: V1 INs function to restrict flexor motor activity and promote active limb extension during stance.
source: In summary, our findings reveal that V1 INs function to (1) restrict flexor motor activity and promote active limb extension during stance and (2) moderate flexion movements during the swing phase of the step cycle.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the V1 IN ablation data.

claim: V1 INs function to moderate flexion movements during the swing phase of the step cycle.
source: In summary, our findings reveal that V1 INs function to (1) restrict flexor motor activity and promote active limb extension during stance and (2) moderate flexion movements during the swing phase of the step cycle.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the V1 IN ablation data.

claim: Activation of channelrhodopsin in V2b INs resulted in a strong and highly selective decrease in extensor-related motor activity as measured by extracellular recordings from the L5 ventral root.
source: However, upon activating channelrhodopsin in V2b INs, there was a strong and highly selective decrease in extensor-related motor activity as measured by extracellular recordings from the L5 ventral root (Figure 7B–D, bar).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 7B–D.

claim: L2 flexor-related motor activity remained largely unchanged following V2b IN activation.
source: By contrast, L2 flexor-related motor activity remained largely unchanged following V2b IN activation, although there was some disturbance in the coherence of the motor rhythm.
evidence: This is stated directly based on optogenetic experiments.

claim: Activation of V1 INs completely suppressed L2 flexor-related and L5 extensor-related rhythmic bursting.
source: Activation of V1 INs had a more pronounced effect on the motor rhythm, in that it completely suppressed L2 flexor-related and L5 extensor-related rhythmic bursting (Figure 7E, bar, n = 5/5 cords).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 7E.

claim: The complete suppression of motor activity by V1 IN activation is likely due to the activation of Renshaw cells.
source: This is likely to be due to the activation of Renshaw cells, which are known to strongly inhibit motor neurons (Windhorst, 1996; Bhumbra et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A greater number of putative V1 IN inhibitory synapses contact flexor motor neuron pools as compared to their antagonist extensor-related motor pools.
source: Quantification of V1- or V2b-IN-derived inhibitory contacts on the soma/proximal dendrites of defined hindlimb motor neurons (n = 12 motor neurons per pool). A greater number of putative V1 IN inhibitory synapses contact flexor motor neuron pools as compared to their antagonist extensor-related motor pools.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 8C.

claim: V2b-derived contacts represent a greater proportion of the inhibitory synapses onto extensor-related motor neurons as compared to antagonist flexor-related motor neurons.
source: In contrast, V2b-derived contacts represent a greater proportion of the inhibitory synapses onto extensor-related motor neurons as compared to antagonist flexor-related motor neurons.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 8C.

claim: There was an approximate twofold greater number of V1-derived synaptic contacts onto TA motor neurons as compared to their antagonist GS counterparts.
source: In comparing V1 inhibitory inputs onto TA and GS motor neurons, we counted an approximate twofold greater number of V1-derived synaptic contacts onto TA motor neurons as compared to their antagonist GS counterparts (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 8B,C.

claim: The proportion of inhibitory contacts onto GS (ankle) extensor motor neurons from V2b INs was higher than the proportion of V2b contacts onto their TA counterparts.
source: Conversely, the proportion of inhibitory contacts onto GS (ankle) extensor motor neurons from V2b INs was higher than the proportion of V2b contacts onto their TA counterparts (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 8C.

claim: Flexor-related motor pools receive proportionately fewer inputs from V2b INs and more from V1 INs.
source: In summary, our findings reveal an overall asymmetry in V1 and V2b in inputs, with flexor-related motor pools receiving proportionately fewer inputs from V2b INs and more from V1 INs, while V2b INs exhibit a bias toward extensor-related motor pools.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the anatomical data.

claim: V2b INs exhibit a bias toward extensor-related motor pools.
source: In summary, our findings reveal an overall asymmetry in V1 and V2b in inputs, with flexor-related motor pools receiving proportionately fewer inputs from V2b INs and more from V1 INs, while V2b INs exhibit a bias toward extensor-related motor pools.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the anatomical data.

claim: V1 and V2b INs contribute to the functional antagonism of limb movements via their differential actions on limb flexor–extensor motor activity.
source: This study defines, for the first time, the functional contribution that V1 and V2b INs make to flexor–extensor motor behaviors in awake behaving mice by showing that these two inhibitory neuron classes contribute to the functional antagonism of limb movements via their differential actions on limb flexor–extensor motor activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: V1 INs restrict flexor-related motor activity during the stance phase of the step cycle to promote full extension of the limb.
source: V1 INs restrict flexor-related motor activity during the stance phase of the step cycle to promote full extension of the limb, whereas V2b INs limit extensor activity to facilitate normal leg flexion movements and the transition to swing.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the functional data.

claim: V2b INs limit extensor activity to facilitate normal leg flexion movements and the transition to swing.
source: V1 INs restrict flexor-related motor activity during the stance phase of the step cycle to promote full extension of the limb, whereas V2b INs limit extensor activity to facilitate normal leg flexion movements and the transition to swing.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the functional data.

claim: The control of limb flexion and extension movements by the V1 and V2b INs is likely to be exerted by graded rather than absolute differences in the inhibition of antagonist motor neurons.
source: Our results also reveal that the control of limb flexion and extension movements by the V1 and V2b INs is likely to be exerted by graded rather than absolute differences in the inhibition of antagonist motor neurons by V1 and V2b INs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the anatomical and functional data.

claim: V1 INs facilitate the transition from swing to stance.
source: Our results demonstrate that V1 INs facilitate the transition from swing to stance, and V2b INs facilitate the transition from stance to swing.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the functional data.

claim: V2b INs facilitate the transition from stance to swing.
source: Our results demonstrate that V1 INs facilitate the transition from swing to stance, and V2b INs facilitate the transition from stance to swing.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the functional data.

claim: In the Xenopus tadpole, V1 (aIN) cells promote the transition between the active and inactive phases of the swimming rhythm by providing early phase inhibition to motor neurons.
source: In the Xenopus tadpole, V1 (aIN) cells promote the transition between the active and inactive phases of the swimming rhythm by providing early phase inhibition to motor neurons (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: The CiA cells, which are homologous to the V1 INs, are likely to function in a similar fashion in zebrafish.
source: The CiA cells, which are homologous to the V1 INs, are likely to function in a similar fashion in zebrafish (Higashijima et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: The absence of resetting deletions suggests both V1 and V2b populations belong to the pattern forming, rather than rhythm generating, layer of the locomotor CPG.
source: The absence of resetting deletions suggests both populations belong to the pattern forming, rather than rhythm generating, layer of the locomotor CPG.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the deletion patterns observed.

claim: The differential silencing of V1 and V2b inhibitory cell populations may contribute to the valence of corrective reflexes such as the stumbling corrective reaction and crossed extension reflex.
source: Moreover, the opposing nature of the deletions that occur when V1 vs V2b INs are inactivated suggests that the differential silencing of these two inhibitory cell populations may contribute to the valence of corrective reflexes such as the stumbling corrective reaction (Forssberg, 1979) and crossed extension reflex (Sherrington, 1910).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: IaIN and Renshaw cell inhibitory synapses are preferentially located on the soma and proximal dendrites of motor neurons.
source: Although we were unable to score inhibitory contacts on the distal dendrites of motor neurons, studies showing IaIN and Renshaw cell inhibitory synapses are preferentially located on the soma, and proximal dendrites of motor neurons (Brown, 1981; Fyffe, 1991) suggests that the counts we obtained in this study are likely to be a reasonable measure of the density of V1 and V2b inhibitory synaptic contacts on motor neurons.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: Relative differences in the inhibitory drive to motor neurons from the V1 and V2b IN populations may contribute to the opposing actions of V1 and V2b INs on flexor–extensor movements.
source: This in turn suggests that relative differences in the inhibitory drive to motor neurons from the V1 and V2b IN populations may contribute to the opposing actions of V1 and V2b INs on flexor–extensor movements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the anatomical data.

claim: Biased inputs from the V1 and V2b INs would facilitate the graded activation of synergist and antagonist motor neurons.
source: First, biased inputs from the V1 and V2b INs would facilitate the graded activation of synergist and antagonist motor neurons. This graded recruitment of antagonist flexor–extensor motor neurons would be expected to play an important role in modulating limb stiffness and compliance, which is necessary for smooth movements and postural control.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional implications of biased inputs.

claim: The co-innervation of flexor and extensor motor neurons by V1 and V2b INs would enable motor neurons to actively summate and compare inhibitory inputs that are differentially gated by these two inhibitory interneuron populations.
source: Second, the co-innervation of flexor and extensor motor neurons by V1 and V2b INs would enable motor neurons to actively summate and compare inhibitory inputs that are differentially gated by these two inhibitory interneuron populations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional implications of co-innervation.

claim: Motor neurons receive a mixture of tonic and dynamic inhibition during locomotion that together with excitatory inputs regulate motor neuron excitability.
source: There is growing evidence that motor neurons receive a mixture of tonic and dynamic inhibition during locomotion that together with excitatory inputs regulate motor neuron excitability (Berg et al., 2007; Johnson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: Gain modulation and increases in the variability of motor neuron spiking represent an important mechanism for altering the dynamic range of motor neuron activity, so as to produce smooth gradients of muscle force transduction.
source: Consequently, gain modulation and increases in the variability of motor neuron spiking represent an important mechanism for altering the dynamic range of motor neuron activity, so as to produce smooth gradients of muscle force transduction (Kristan, 2007; Johnson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: Inhibitory IaINs are a major source of the tonic inhibitory drive underlying the push–pull control of motor activity in ankle extensor motor neurons.
source: Johnson et al. (2012) have recently shown that inhibitory IaINs are a major source of the tonic inhibitory drive underlying the push–pull control of motor activity in ankle extensor motor neurons.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: V1 and V2b INs are the sole source of Ia inhibition to motor neurons.
source: Our observation that V1 and V2b INs are the sole source of Ia inhibition to motor neurons (Zhang et al., 2014) suggests that they make a major contribution to inhibitory push–pull conductances.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The biased innervation of motor neurons by V1 and V2b INs could facilitate push–pull in limb motor neurons under a range of behavioral conditions.
source: As such, the biased innervation of motor neurons by V1 and V2b INs (Figure 8) could facilitate push–pull in limb motor neurons under a range of behavioral conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional implications of biased innervation.

claim: An inhibitory network comprised of either V1 or V2b INs still generates an alternating pattern of flexor–extensor activity in awake behaving mice, albeit an abnormal one.
source: Our in vivo behavioral analyses showing an inhibitory network comprised of either V1 or V2b INs still generates an alternating pattern of flexor–extensor activity in awake behaving mice, albeit an abnormal one, concurs with our in vitro analysis showing flexor–extensor alternation is only completely degraded when both the V1 and V2b IN populations are inactivated (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the in vivo and in vitro findings.

claim: V1 and V2b INs can function in a redundant manner to produce a grossly alternating flexor–extensor locomotor output.
source: These findings argue that the V1 and V2b INs can function in a redundant manner to produce a grossly alternating flexor–extensor locomotor output, and they are in general agreement with the mixed innervation of flexor and extensor motor neurons by V1 and V2b INs (Figure 8; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional and anatomical data.

claim: The co-innervation of flexor and extensor motor neurons by V1 and V2b INs may contribute to the functional recovery that occurs following V1 or V2b IN ablation.
source: The co-innervation of flexor and extensor motor neurons by V1 and V2b INs may contribute to the functional recovery that occurs following V1 or V2b IN ablation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the recovery observed.

claim: The functional recovery is suggestive of a degree of plasticity in the inhibitory control of flexor–extensor movements by both inhibitory populations.
source: This functional recovery is suggestive of a degree of plasticity in the inhibitory control of flexor–extensor movements by both inhibitory populations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the recovery observed.

claim: The functional deficits that persist after ablating the V1 INs are more pronounced than those found following V2b IN ablation.
source: Interestingly, the functional deficits that persist after ablating the V1 INs are more pronounced than those found following V2b IN ablation.
evidence: This is stated directly based on the behavioral observations.

claim: There are twice as many V1 INs as compared to V2b INs in the lumbar spinal cord.
source: This might be attributable to the relative abundance of these two cell types in the lumbar spinal cord, where there are twice as many V1 INs as compared to V2b INs (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: The motor pools innervating hip and ankle flexors tend to be skewed rostrally in the lumbar spinal cord when compared to their extensor antagonist motor pools.
source: Differences in the axonal morphology of V1 and V2b INs may also contribute to the persistent hindlimb hyperflexion phenotype V1 IN-ablated mice display, as the motor pools innervating hip and ankle flexors tend to be skewed rostrally in the lumbar spinal cord when compared to their extensor antagonist motor pools (McHanwell and Biscoe, 1981; Yakovenko et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: V2b INs predominantly project their axons caudally.
source: In this context, it is worth noting that V2b INs predominantly project their axons caudally (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and may therefore have a limited capacity to substitute for those V1 INs that have rostrally projecting axons.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The transition from stance to swing during walking is controlled in part by Ib pathways from ankle extensor GTOs.
source: This transition is controlled in part by Ib pathways from ankle extensor GTOs (Duysens and Pearson, 1980; Pearson, 2008).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: V2b INs receive inputs from neurons in the dorsal horn.
source: Our characterization of presynaptic inputs to V1 and V2b INs showing the V2b INs receive inputs from neurons in the dorsal horn (F Stam and MG, unpublished findings) is a strong indication that inhibitory IbINs are derived from the V2b IN population.
evidence: This is stated directly and attributed to unpublished findings.

claim: Inhibitory IbINs are derived from the V2b IN population.
source: Our characterization of presynaptic inputs to V1 and V2b INs showing the V2b INs receive inputs from neurons in the dorsal horn (F Stam and MG, unpublished findings) is a strong indication that inhibitory IbINs are derived from the V2b IN population.
evidence: This is an inference based on unpublished data.

claim: The presumed loss of inhibitory IbINs that occurs when V2b INs are ablated could account for the delayed transition from stance to swing.
source: As such, the presumed loss of inhibitory IbINs that occurs when V2b INs are ablated could account for the delayed transition from stance to swing that we observe (Pearson, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Golgi tendon-derived sensory feedback is normally attenuated during swimming.
source: The loss of IbINs in the V2b IN-ablated mice might also explain why these mice do not show any major change in GS and TA muscle activity during swimming, as Golgi tendon-derived sensory feedback is normally attenuated during this activity (Akay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: V1 INs suppress flexor motor activity during the stance/extension phase of walking to ensure proper extension of the limbs.
source: In summary, this study demonstrates that V1 and V2b INs differentially control flexor–extensor motor output, with V1 INs suppressing flexor motor activity during the stance/extension phase of walking to ensure proper extension of the limbs, while the V2b INs suppress extensor activity to facilitate limb extension and ensure the timely transition from stance to swing.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings.

claim: V2b INs suppress extensor activity to facilitate limb extension and ensure the timely transition from stance to swing.
source: In summary, this study demonstrates that V1 and V2b INs differentially control flexor–extensor motor output, with V1 INs suppressing flexor motor activity during the stance/extension phase of walking to ensure proper extension of the limbs, while the V2b INs suppress extensor activity to facilitate limb extension and ensure the timely transition from stance to swing.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings.

claim: V1 and V2b INs contribute to the dynamic control of limb movements during walking via their differential effects on flexor and extensor motor activity.
source: Our results are consistent with the V1 and V2b INs contributing to the dynamic control of limb movements during walking via their differential effects on flexor and extensor motor activity.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings.

claim: The V1 and V2b IN populations are made up of multiple cell types.
source: It should be noted that the V1 and V2b IN populations are made up of multiple cell types and the respective contribution that each of these cell types make to flexor–extensor-driven behaviors needs to be assessed.
evidence: This is stated directly as a caveat to the findings.
